  • 23, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Cisco (NASDAQ: CSCO) and OpenAI today introduced an open source effort to make infrastructure secure by default and able to defend itself against today's sophisticated cyber attacks.
  • According to recent reports, defenders must protect every part of their infrastructure, all the time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An industry-first open source project, Shirudo, helps systems defend themselves at machine speed.

SAN JOSE, Calif., Nov. 23, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Cisco (NASDAQ: CSCO) and OpenAI today introduced an open source effort to make infrastructure secure by default and able to defend itself against today's sophisticated cyber attacks. For too long, security has been a coat of paint. Cisco builds protection into the infrastructure itself, drawing on decades of building and protecting the systems the world depends on. OpenAI brings leading frontier AI research and insight into the attacks coming next. Together, they combine their insight to help anticipate AI-driven threats with the control to stop them.

According to recent reports, defenders must protect every part of their infrastructure, all the time. Attackers only need one machine that hasn't been patched. Shirudo is an important step toward closing that gap. The goal is infrastructure that is hardened from the moment it is built, keeps getting harder to attack, and can be restored to a known-good state if it is compromised.

In a recent development, "There is nothing more crucial than giving security teams the tools they need to match the speed of the AI-driven threats they are facing. We need self-defending infrastructure that acts at the speed of code, learns in real time, and shields itself until patches are safely rolled out," stated Jeetu Patel, Cisco President and Chief Product Officer. "Today, we're proud to announce Shirudo with OpenAI, an important step towards that vision as we continue to collaborate with the wider community to solve the unique challenges of AI safety and security.".

Recent findings suggest that "We're giving defenders better models and tools to find and fix vulnerabilities faster, but finding a bug today doesn't mean you can patch every system tomorrow," said Greg Brockman, President and Co-founder of OpenAI. "We are partnering closely with Cisco on Shirudo to help teams protect the systems they need to keep running while they build and roll out a fix. So many teams rely on the same software that it makes sense to build these tools in the open. Now when one team finds a better way to protect a system, others don't have to start from scratch.".

It has been revealed that shirudo: An Open Source Project from Cisco and OpenAIShirudo, Japanese for "shield," uses eBPF, a technology that runs small, custom programs inside the operating system kernel without changing its source code. With it, AI agents can find a vulnerability, build a shield, and test that it stops the attack without disrupting the service. Shields go live only when the evidence notes they are safe. Every shield is cryptographically signed, so the host can verify it before it runs, even if an attacker has gained administrator access.

In testing against recent critical vulnerabilities "Java4shell" and the PHP flaw, Shirudo was able to write code that detected and blocked attempts to exploit both threats. By utilizing an agentic framework, Shirudo matches the speed of AI-driven attacks as soon as a vulnerability is identified. Learn more about Shirudo here.

Cisco and OpenAI are inviting developers, researchers, and enterprises to help shape what comes next. Contribute a test that reproduces a vulnerability, run a shield against a kernel build you use, or show us where it breaks legitimate traffic. To learn more about Shirudo, visit: https://github.com/shirudo-dev/shirudo.

With purpose at its core, Cisco remains committed to creating a more connected and inclusive future for all. Discover more on The Newsroom and follow us on X at @Cisco.

Non-QM lending grows as buyers change financing strategies

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (560 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Homebuyers are increasingly willing to change their mortgage financing strategies to get into the housing market, helping drive growth in nonqualified mortgage (non-QM) lending according to latest research from Cotality.
  • Recent findings suggest that data presented during a Cotality webinar last week found that 69% of buyers initially cut lifestyle spending to make homeownership more affordable.
  • The findings point to growing demand for alternative mortgage products.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Homebuyers are increasingly willing to change their mortgage financing strategies to get into the housing market, helping drive growth in nonqualified mortgage (non-QM) lending according to latest research from Cotality.

Recent findings suggest that data presented during a Cotality webinar last week found that 69% of buyers initially cut lifestyle spending to make homeownership more affordable. But once these adjustments become insufficient, 65% turn to changing their financing options, according to the manufacturer’s analysis of homebuyer behavior.

The findings point to growing demand for alternative mortgage products.

According to recent reports, “The economy and the way people earn income has changed,” noted Selma Hepp, chief economist at Cotality. “Non-QM is becoming a permanent component of the mortgage market because the borrower base it serves is permanent.”.

In a recent development, hepp pointed to the growing number of business owners, independent contractors, commission-based workers, real estate investors and households with multiple income sources. She cited approximately 11.9 million independent contractors, representing 7.4% of employment, and 9 million multiple-job holders, representing 5.5% of employed people.

According to recent reports, many of these borrowers may have the financial resources to repay a mortgage but struggle to demonstrate their income through conventional underwriting. But Hepp cautioned that alternative underwriting should not be presented as a simple affordability solution. “What it can do is align underwriting more closely with what the borrower’s actual financial capacity is,” she mentioned.

Nonagency lending has expanded in recent years, driven primarily by non-QM loans, stated Patrick Kaiser, Cotality’s principal product manager in property intelligence.

Recent findings suggest that kaiser mentioned non-QM lending was on pace to exceed 2025 volume by the end of 2026 and could grow again in 2027 if current trends continue. Loans for consumer borrowers remain the largest share of the market, but debt-service-coverage ratio (DSCR) loans for real estate investors are gaining ground.

Sources indicate that investor lending brings its own risks. Rising insurance premiums, property taxes and other operating costs can weaken rental-property cash flow, Hepp remarked. A softer labor market could also put pressure on borrowers with self-employment or variable income.

But Holly Niemeier, a senior loan officer at NEXA Lending who works primarily with investors, told HousingWire that investor demand has kept her busy despite elevated borrowing costs. Her clients range from first-time investors to those with hundreds of properties, including some looking to acquire as many as 20 at a time.

In a recent development, “People are having a hard time getting loans, and the investors now, the prices have dropped some, so I’m busier than I’ve ever been this month,” she mentioned. “The rates aren’t really affecting the investors. They’re still buying.”.

Niemeier said investors use different strategies depending on their available capital. Some buy properties with cash, renovate them and refinance, while others purchase turnkey rentals with existing tenants. Those who run low on capital may use hard money loans to acquire and renovate properties before refinancing into DSCR loans.

Recent findings suggest that virtually all of Niemeier’s investor business involves DSCR financing, either for individual properties or through portfolio loans. She also sees investors favoring lower-cost properties in urban markets such as St. Louis and Detroit, where smaller down payments can make it easier to expand a portfolio.

Recent findings suggest that “The investors don’t seem to flinch,” she said. “They don’t change anything.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 16:29 EST / NOVEMBER 23 2026.

In a recent development, crowdStrike Holdings Inc. today announced prepares to acquire Zscaler Inc., a fellow provider of cybersecurity software, for about $43.9 billion.

It has been revealed that the all-stock deal values the latter company at $260.40 per share. That’s a 34% premium to Zscaler’s closing price on Friday, the day CrowdStrike’s takeover interest became public. The transaction would be the largest cybersecurity acquisition on record by a wide margin.

It has been revealed that investors weren’t entirely thrilled. CrowdStrike’s shares fell 9% today, an indication that might think it’s an awfully large pill to swallow. Zscaler’s stock, however, rose almost 18%.

The companies reported their quarterly results in conjunction with the acquisition announcement. Both topped expectations across the board. CrowdStrike posted adjusted net income of $354.9 million on $1.58 billion in revenue, while Zscaler reported a $208.4 million adjusted profit and sales of $949.3 million. The former company also boosted its full-year guidance.

CrowdStrike’s flagship Falcon platform uses lightweight programs called sensors to protect employee devices, cloud instances and other technology assets. Zscaler’s Zero Trust Exchange, in turn, protects the network connections that link together those assets. The platform is positioned as an alternative to virtual private network tools.

It has been revealed that the product portfolios of CrowdStrike’s and Zscaler overlap in some areas. Both companies offer tools that can protect artificial intelligence applications from threats such as prompt injections. They also compete in the secure browser category, although their respective offerings take different approaches to blocking malware.

According to recent reports, zscaler offers a tool that can automatically launch simulated cyberattacks against applications to find weak points. CrowdStrike joined the fray as well earlier this year with SafeMind, a set of custom AI models and related assets. It not only finds software vulnerabilities but also develops detections, automated workflows designed to spot hacking attempts.

CrowdStrike mentioned that it will use the network telemetry collected by Zscaler to enhance SafeMind’s training dataset. In 2024, the latter tech giant disclosed that its platform blocked more than 9 billion threats per day. That activity, which has no doubt grown in volume since, should give CrowdStrike’s AI models a more complete understanding of hacker behavior.

It has been revealed that the company’s aims for Zscaler also extend beyond AI training. CrowdStrike will incorporate the network protection provider’s software into its Flex offering, which enables customers to buy multiple cybersecurity tools via a single contract. That could help expand the adoption of Zscaler’s products among CrowdStrike customers.

It has been revealed that the companies have also identified other upselling opportunities. They disclosed today that about 8,000 Zscaler customers don’t yet use CrowdStrike products.

“With Zscaler, we’re building cybersecurity’s operating system: a single control plane to deploy AI, control AI, and enable any agentic application to run safely,” remarked CrowdStrike founder and Chief Executive Officer George Kurtz (pictured). “We see a path to become the largest AI safety and security tech giant the world has ever seen.”.

Recent findings suggest that crowdStrike expects to complete the acquisition in the second half of its 2028 fiscal year, which starts next February. The organization stated that the deal will be “significantly and immediately accretive” to free cash flow per share upon closing.

CrowdStrike expects Zscaler’s financial impact to grow over time. It estimates that the deal will unlock $500 million worth of annual cost synergies within 18 to 24 months, mainly in the form of data center, supplier and operational improvements. The manufacturer also sees Zscaler boosting its annual revenue run-rate by $1 billion within 30 months.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Leading the Army Readiness Council, Brito brings 38 years of Army training and readiness leadership as national security systems move to post-quantum cryptography.

MIAMI, Nov. 23, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Gen. Gary M. Brito, U.S. Army (Ret.), the 18th and final commanding general of U.S. Army Training and Doctrine Command (TRADOC), has joined Qtonic Quantum to lead the Army Readiness Council and serve as Senior Military Advisor to the Founders. His appointment comes 39 days before NSA's CNSA 2.0 compliance date for fresh national security system acquisitions.

Sources indicate that under CNSSP 15 and NSA's CNSA 2.0 guidance, all upcoming national security system acquisitions are required to be CNSA 2.0 compliant, meaning quantum-resistant, by Jan. 1, 2027. NIST finalized its first post-quantum cryptography standards, FIPS 203, 204 and 205, in August 2024. Adversaries can harvest encrypted data today and decrypt it once quantum computers mature.

Sources indicate that brito retired as a four-star general after a 38-year Army career. At TRADOC he led the command responsible for the Army's institutional training, education and leader development. He also led the strategy, planning and early integration of TRADOC's merger with Army Futures Command, which culminated in the activation of the new U.S. Army Transformation and Training Command in October 2025. He previously commanded the Maneuver Center of Excellence and Fort Benning and the Joint Readiness Training Center and Fort Polk, served as the Army's 49th Deputy Chief of Staff, G-1, the Army's senior human resources officer, and deployed to Iraq and Afghanistan.

As leader of the Army Readiness Council, Brito will drive the council's work on how post-quantum migration is planned and measured as a readiness problem across Army and joint environments. He will also advise the founders on how Qtonic Quantum serves defense and government leaders. He serves in a personal capacity, and his views do not represent the Department of the Army or the Department of War. He joins a team that includes senior retired military leaders.

It has been revealed that "Readiness is built, not declared," remarked Lt. Gen. (Ret.) Roger L. Cloutier Jr., former commander of NATO Allied Land Command and Founding Chair of the Allied Defense Council at Qtonic Quantum. "General Brito spent 38 years building it at the scale of an institution. Post-quantum migration is a readiness problem, and he will help us put evidence in front of the leaders who set the schedule.".

In a recent development, "Leaders at all levels are charged to ensure unit readiness against all threats," said Brito. "Communications and data readiness is no different. Leaders need to inventory what they depend on, test it and fix it on a schedule they set, not one an adversary sets.".

Qtonic Quantum's Find. Prove. Fix. approach starts with QScout Gold, which delivers quantum cyber risk and vulnerability intelligence, a crypto-agility assessment and a signed cryptographic bill of materials (CBOM). Together they give leaders an evidence-backed inventory of the cryptography their systems depend on.

Brito holds a bachelor's degree from Penn State University, where the Penn State Alumni Association named him a 2025 Alumni Fellow, and a master's degree in human resource management from Troy University.

Breaking: Sometimes the most valuable data is the house nobody bought

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Canceled listing data in the MLS can reveal where buyers noted no.
  • When agents sit down to price a listing, we know the drill: Pull the solds.
  • But there’s another category of data sitting right there in the MLS that we frequently overlook: the houses nobody bought.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Want to price more precisely? Canceled listing data in the MLS can reveal where buyers noted no. Learn three steps to add failed listings to your next CMA.

When agents sit down to price a listing, we know the drill: Pull the solds. Look at what’s coming soon, active and pending. Adjust for condition, location, square footage and amenities. Figure out where our house fits.

But there’s another category of data sitting right there in the MLS that we frequently overlook: the houses nobody bought.

In a recent development, expired. Canceled. Withdrawn. Earlier in my career, I looked at these failed listings all the time. Then the market changed. When inventory became tight, and buyers were competing for homes, digging through failed listings often wasn’t necessary to determine where a property would sell.

Now the market is shifting again; pricing must be more precise, and I’m sharpening my approach by bringing an old tool back into my pricing process.

In a recent development, A sold comp tells us where a buyer said yes, but a failed listing can help us figure out where buyers said no. And in a buyer-favored market, that’s valuable information.

According to recent reports, imagine you’re pricing a home, and the recent comparable sales range from $600,000 to $625,000. Then you expand your search.

Suddenly, you know considerably more than the sold comps alone told you. Other sellers have already tested the upper limits of pricing, and buyers responded. It’s essentially a series of pricing experiments someone else conducted for you — and they paid the carrying costs.

Recent findings suggest that one of the most interesting things buried in MLS history is the pricing journey. A property might show a final list price of $649,000 and an eventual sale of $630,000. Dig deeper, and you may discover this:.

$725,000 → $699,000 → $675,000 → canceled → relisted at $649,000 → sold for $630,000.

That’s a different story. The sale tells us what one buyer eventually paid. The listing history tells us buyers had previously rejected that house at $725,000, $699,000 and $675,000.

According to recent reports, it also illustrates something sellers don’t always understand: Getting to the right price eventually isn’t necessarily the same as pricing correctly from the beginning. After months of market exposure and multiple reductions, buyers may stop asking, “Could this be the house?” They start asking, “What’s wrong with it?”.

According to recent reports, when I find a comparable property that sat for 90 days without selling, I want to know what did sell during those same 90 days. Sometimes we blame the market when the market was functioning just fine. Buyers were buying houses. They simply weren’t buying that one.

It has been revealed that maybe they chose the renovated house at $640,000. Maybe they paid $650,000 for the better lot. They may have even paid more for another property because it offered something the failed listing didn’t. That’s useful information when you’re sitting across from a seller who believes buyers just need more time to appreciate their home.

If buyers repeatedly toured the property and purchased competing homes instead, the market may already have delivered its opinion.

Industry observers note that this is where agents have to resist oversimplifying the data. An expired listing isn’t automatic proof that a house was overpriced, and a canceled listing certainly isn’t either.

Listings fail for all sorts of reasons. Sellers change their minds. Job transfers fall through. Repairs surface. Agents get fired. Sometimes a seller receives a perfectly acceptable offer and decides not to move.

So, investigate. Call the previous agent. I might simply say:.

“I’m pricing a similar property and noticed yours was on the market last year. Is there anything you can tell me about the activity or why the seller decided not to continue?”.

Twenty-seven showings and no offers tell me something. Two showings in four months tells me something different.

There’s one more number worth considering: the cost of the pricing journey.

Recent findings suggest that find a house that started high, sat, reduced, expired, relisted and eventually sold. Then compare it with similar homes that entered the market closer to where buyers were actually buying.

In a recent development, sellers often view aspirational pricing as a no-risk strategy: “We can always come down.” Technically, that’s true. But time isn’t free, and neither is market perception.

The next time you’re preparing a CMA in a shifting or buyer-favored market:.

Sources indicate that we’re very good at studying success in real estate. But as pricing gets harder, I’ve found myself returning to an old habit: studying the failures, too. Sold listings tell us where buyers have been willing to say yes. Sometimes the house nobody bought is the one that tells us exactly where they started saying no.

Roxanne Hale is the associate broker of the Art House Team, brokered by RealtySouth in Birmingham, Alabama. Get connected on Facebook or YouTube.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Fresh York’s governor has joined the growing lists of state lawmakers enacting laws to govern the use of private listing networks.
  • On Friday, Governor Kathy Hochul signed Senate Bill S10274, also known as the “Fair and Transparent Real Estate Listings Act,” into law, just seven days after it was delivered to her desk.
  • The legislation was first introduced in mid-March before going on to pass the Assembly in late May and the state Senate on June 1, 2026.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Fresh York’s governor has joined the growing lists of state lawmakers enacting laws to govern the use of private listing networks.

On Friday, Governor Kathy Hochul signed Senate Bill S10274, also known as the “Fair and Transparent Real Estate Listings Act,” into law, just seven days after it was delivered to her desk.

The legislation was first introduced in mid-March before going on to pass the Assembly in late May and the state Senate on June 1, 2026.

According to recent reports, the law requires residential listings to be publicly advertised or marketed on platforms that are accessible to the general public. According to the law, this means that the publication, platform or website the listing is advertised on does not require payment or for the consumer to work with a certain brokerage or agent in order to view the property information. Additionally, the law specifies that any licensed real estate broker or agent working with a buyer without limitation to a particular brokerage, franchise, or select group of licensees should also be able to view information about the listing.

Here’s how it will impact real estate professionals and brokerages:.

Despite this emphasis on ensuring listing information is easily accessible, the law does note that sellers who sign a state-provided standardized disclosure form explaining the risks and tradeoffs associated with non-public marketing, may withhold their listing from public marketing.

In the disclosure included in the text of the law, sellers must acknowledge that their property “may not be marketed or distributed outside the real estate brokerage that the listing agent is associated with through mass-marketing channels,” and that due to this, the seller understands that the reduced exposure of the property may lead to a reduction in the number of offers they receive, potentially negatively impacting their ability to sell the house.

Industry observers note that those who break this law can be fined up to $5,000. In addition, under the law, the Department of State may suspend or revoke a real estate professional’s license. The law is set to go into effect in late May 2027.

Bess Freedman, the CEO of Newly introduced York City-based Brown Harris Stevens, a RealTrends Verified brokerage,  is celebrating the passage of the law.

“Buying a home shouldn’t depend on who you know or which brokerage you work with. I’m proud that Latest York is taking on private listing networks and making public marketing the standard,” Freedman wrote in an emailed statement. “Buyers deserve to see what’s available and choose who represents them. Sellers deserve the chance to reach the widest possible audience, and those who want privacy — a choice that has always existed — can still choose it with a clear understanding of what they may give up.”.

In addition to Freedman, Caroline Burton, the general manager of StreetEasy, which is owned by Zillow, is also applauding the news and thanking the state legislature for “putting consumers first.”.

“When homes are kept out of public view, New Yorkers lose out, especially in a market where homes for sale are already scarce,” Burton wrote in an emailed statement. “Finding a home in the most challenging market shouldn’t depend on privilege, who you know or who you work with. In one of the biggest decisions in a person’s life, New Yorkers deserve an open and transparent marketplace so they can make an informed choice. This is a win for all buyers, sellers, and the agents who serve them.”.

Beyond these two firms, which had been vocal proponents of listing transparency, Compass International Holdings, which has been promoting its three-phased marketing proposal, which includes a private listing phase, is also praising the enacting of the law.

A Compass spokesperson told HousingWire that the upcoming law “preserves homeowners’ right to choose how they market their homes,” which includes marketing the property through Compass’s See It First initiative. Compass debuted See It First in September. The company stated it is intended to expand inventory visibility for buyers, allow sellers to “test and learn” without public days on market and provide agents with an additional marketing lever.

“See It First early access homes comply with the fresh law and continue to give sellers flexibility in how and when they bring their homes to market,” a Compass spokesperson told HousingWire via email.

Similarly, the New York State Association of Realtors (NYSAR) said in a statement that the “legislation strikes an appropriate balance between promoting transparency and protecting consumer choice by preserving the ability of property owners to determine how their properties are marketed.”.

“This fresh law helps ensure that property owners are fully informed of the potential consequences of limiting the public marketing of their properties, including the possibility of reduced exposure to prospective buyers or tenants,” the statement read.

In a recent development, in enacting this law, New York is joining Connecticut, Wisconsin and Washington in creating a law governing the public marketing of residential properties. New York’s law is similar to the ones passed in Connecticut and Wisconsin, both of which provide sellers the ability to opt-out of public marketing with a signed disclosure. The Washington law, however, does not include a pathway for sellers to opt-out of public marketing besides a health or safety concern. These laws are at the moment in effect in Connecticut and Wisconsin, with Washington’s law slated to go into effect on Jan. 1, 2027.

Make it 8: Connecticut joins first responder homebuying push

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Connecticut is the latest state to help first responders reach their homeownership goals with assistance for down payments and closing costs.
  • The “First Responders’ Time to Own” program gives state and local police officers, full-time and volunteer firefighters and emergency medical service personnel $25,000 in forgivable assistance through the Connecticut Housing Finance Authority (CHFA) and the Connecticut Department of Housing.
  • In addition to down payment and closing cost help, the program gives applicants a 0.125 percentage point interest rate reduction on their CHFA first mortgage.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Connecticut is the latest state to help first responders reach their homeownership goals with assistance for down payments and closing costs.

The “First Responders’ Time to Own” program gives state and local police officers, full-time and volunteer firefighters and emergency medical service personnel $25,000 in forgivable assistance through the Connecticut Housing Finance Authority (CHFA) and the Connecticut Department of Housing. To qualify, first responders must have completed two years of service and purchase a primary residence within the community they serve.

In addition to down payment and closing cost help, the program gives applicants a 0.125 percentage point interest rate reduction on their CHFA first mortgage.

Sources indicate that “Connecticut’s police officers, firefighters and EMS personnel dedicate themselves to protecting our families and communities, and we want to make sure they have the opportunity to build their own futures here,” Governor Ned Lamont stated in a prepared statement on Tuesday. “By helping reduce one of the biggest barriers to buying a home, we’re investing in the people who serve our state and the communities that depend on them.”.

The program is part of Public Act 26-12, a state bill that aims to increase the number of first responders with a number of incentives, including college tuition reimbursement and improved labor protections.

“The people who protect and serve our communities should be able to afford to live in those communities, and this program with help them do it,” Comptroller Sean Scanlon noted in a written statement. “Helping the people who put their lives on the line for us every day buy their first home is literally the least we can do, and I’m proud to have worked with Governor Lamont and legislature to make this a reality.”.

Seven other states also have down payment assistance programs for first responders. Florida, Nevada, Georgia and South Carolina provide flat amounts, ranging from $10,000 to $35,000. Texas, Maryland and Ohio’s programs are percentage-based and offer assistance ranging from 2.5 percent to 5 percent of the purchase price.

The terms of each program vary. Most states forgive the assistance after five to seven years, but Nevada requires homebuyers to repay the funds within 30 years. And like Connecticut, Ohio also offers a 0.25 percent mortgage rate discount.

In a recent development, “Homeownership offers more than a place to live. It creates stability, strengthens connections to community and provides an opportunity to build wealth over time,” CHFA CEO and Executive Director Nandini Natarajan said in an announcement. “Through First Responders’ Time to Own, we’re helping the people who answer the call for our communities take an important step toward achieving their own homeownership goals.”.

First responders often fall through the cracks of housing assistance programs because they don’t earn enough to afford market-rate housing but earn too much to qualify for federal housing vouchers.

In a recent development, inman explored this dilemma last September in a feature on workforce housing in resort towns like Jackson Hole, Vail and Tahoe. These towns can’t operate without first responders and other essential workers in the hospitality and retail sectors. However, rental and for-sale home prices have far outpaced what these workers earn, forcing them to commute long distances from more affordable towns or take on second and third jobs to survive.

It has been revealed that the solution for some of these towns has been investing in workforce housing, which caps prices for households that earn between 60 percent and 120 percent of their area’s AMI. Most workforce housing is rent-only, but some states are extending the programs to include for-sale properties.

In a recent development, “I think the fact that workforce housing can be necessary or is a thing in the first place is really an indictment of the state of housing affordability in the country today,” Realtor.com Senior Economist Jake Krimmel remarked. “I think it’s important to ground any conversation about workforce and affordable housing in that reality. It’s a market failure and a policy failure that someone could be a doctor, a teacher or another kind of professional and cannot afford to pay the market rent or own a home outright.”.

Windermere Principal Economist Jeff Tucker noted workforce housing isn’t a panacea for affordability and works within an ecosystem of other housing and economic policies, such as upzoning, to create a more equitable market.

Sources indicate that tucker’s comments came a month after the Senate introduced the ROAD to Housing Act of 2025, and three months before the House introduced the Housing for the 21st Century Act. The bills were eventually combined into the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, which passed in June.

“A broad package of necessary reforms to make more housing construction possible in much of the country is a really important component of a long-term solution to the housing affordability challenges we face,” Tucker said. “Our current housing shortage took years to develop. So it’ll take years to build our way out of it.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Washington Department of Financial Institutions (DFI) has ordered Directors Mortgage to temporarily stop taking on newly introduced business in the state, including the origination of loans for Washington residents or for properties located in the state, citing exam interference and concerns about the firm’s finances.

It has been revealed that according to the DFI’s order, examiners who conducted an on-site review at the Oregon-based lender’s main office from Nov. 17 to Nov. 19 were not provided requested information and records. During that period, the department served a subpoena on the company’s CEO and owner to obtain the production of original books, accounts, papers, records and files.

The department also mentioned it obtained information during the examination indicating that the company was not meeting its financial obligations to employees or third-party vendors.

“Respondent’s failure to comply with the Department’s examination authority and Respondent’s current financial condition pose a serious risk of injury to the public,” the order states.

A representative of Directors Mortgage did not immediately respond to HousingWire’s request for comment.

The emergency order, signed on Friday by Brian J. Guerard, Washington DFI’s acting director, requires Directors Mortgage to deliver detailed financial information, including balance sheets and bank account data, and to fully respond to the department’s subpoena. The order also directs the tech giant to satisfy outstanding financial obligations.

It has been revealed that under Washington law, companies may contest such orders in an administrative hearing. If a respondent does not seek a hearing, the order becomes permanent when DFI issues a final order.

Directors Mortgage, founded in 1998 by president and CEO Mark J. Hanna and headquartered in Oregon, has originated about $235 million in mortgages year to date, according to InGenius. The organization had roughly 40 loan officers and nine active branches as of Monday, per data from the Nationwide Multistate Licensing System.

Washington’s DFI has been active recently regarding mortgage enforcement. Newrez recently agreed to pay roughly $3 million and implement wide-ranging mortgage servicing changes to resolve allegations by the department that it engaged in unfair or deceptive acts or practices.

Earlier this year, Washington state regulators issued a $75,000 fine and a $3,000 investigation fee against West Capital Lending, alleging multiple violations of the state’s consumer loan act. The organization was accused of allowing unlicensed individuals to conduct mortgage-related activities and of failing to meet certain disclosure and reporting requirements. Per the agreement, WCL did not admit to the allegations nor any wrongdoing.

Sources indicate that meanwhile, Rocket Mortgage and Mr. Cooper Group recently agreed to pay a combined $6.75 million to the Latest York State Department of Financial Services to resolve allegations of cybersecurity violations tied to data protection, risk assessments and incident reporting.

Cisco and OpenAI Launch Shirudo, A New Project to Safeguard Agentic AI

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (765 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Prnewswire

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An industry-first open source project, Shirudo, helps systems defend themselves at machine speed.
  • 23, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Cisco (NASDAQ: CSCO) and OpenAI today introduced an open source effort to make infrastructure secure by default and able to defend itself against today's sophisticated cyber attacks.
  • Defenders must protect every part of their infrastructure, all the time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An industry-first open source project, Shirudo, helps systems defend themselves at machine speed.

SAN JOSE, Calif., Nov. 23, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Cisco (NASDAQ: CSCO) and OpenAI today introduced an open source effort to make infrastructure secure by default and able to defend itself against today's sophisticated cyber attacks. For too long, security has been a coat of paint. Cisco builds protection into the infrastructure itself, drawing on decades of building and protecting the systems the world depends on. OpenAI brings leading frontier AI research and insight into the attacks coming next. Together, they combine their insight to help anticipate AI-driven threats with the control to stop them.

Defenders must protect every part of their infrastructure, all the time. Attackers only need one machine that hasn't been patched. Shirudo is an vital step toward closing that gap. The goal is infrastructure that is hardened from the moment it is built, keeps getting harder to attack, and can be restored to a known-good state if it is compromised.

"There is nothing more important than giving security teams the tools they need to match the speed of the AI-driven threats they are facing. We need self-defending infrastructure that acts at the speed of code, learns in real time, and shields itself until patches are safely rolled out," said Jeetu Patel, Cisco President and Chief Product Officer. "Today, we're proud to announce Shirudo with OpenAI, an important step towards that vision as we continue to collaborate with the wider community to solve the unique challenges of AI safety and security.".

"We're giving defenders better models and tools to find and fix vulnerabilities faster, but finding a bug today doesn't mean you can patch every system tomorrow," remarked Greg Brockman, President and Co-founder of OpenAI. "We are partnering closely with Cisco on Shirudo to help teams protect the systems they need to keep running while they build and roll out a fix. So many teams rely on the same software that it makes sense to build these tools in the open. Now when one team finds a better way to protect a system, others don't have to start from scratch.".

Shirudo: An Open Source Project from Cisco and OpenAIShirudo, Japanese for "shield," uses eBPF, a technology that runs small, custom programs inside the operating system kernel without changing its source code. With it, AI agents can find a vulnerability, build a shield, and test that it stops the attack without disrupting the service. Shields go live only when the evidence indicates they are safe. Every shield is cryptographically signed, so the host can verify it before it runs, even if an attacker has gained administrator access.

Industry observers note that in testing against recent critical vulnerabilities "Java4shell" and the PHP flaw, Shirudo was able to write code that detected and blocked attempts to exploit both threats. By utilizing an agentic framework, Shirudo matches the speed of AI-driven attacks as soon as a vulnerability is identified. Learn more about Shirudo here.

According to recent reports, cisco and OpenAI are inviting developers, researchers, and enterprises to help shape what comes next. Contribute a test that reproduces a vulnerability, run a shield against a kernel build you use, or show us where it breaks legitimate traffic. To learn more about Shirudo, visit: https://github.com/shirudo-dev/shirudo.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Artificial intelligence is helping mortgage lenders and due-diligence firms review loan files and extract borrower information, but integrating AI into underwriting processes isn’t a one-and-done experience. The technology still needs human oversight, experts say, especially when loans involve unusual circumstances or require judgment beyond standard guidelines.

It has been revealed that at Incenter Diligence Solutions, AI has accelerated document indexing and data extraction, according to president Pamela Hamrick. Technology can now sort and categorize thousands of pages of loan documents in minutes, replacing a process that once required employees to manually separate and label files.

According to recent reports, hamrick said that while AI can extract information from standardized mortgage documents like loan estimates and closing disclosures, borrower-provided records — including pay stubs and bank statements. — are harder to process because their formats vary.

AI, however, can identify inconsistencies across documents and summarize them for underwriters to investigate.

“The technology is identifying the questions, and the inconsistencies and the anomalies, between all of this documentation, and summarizing that for an underwriter or a reviewer … to dig deeper and make a decision about whether or not what the AI has identified is a real risk — or if it’s a minimal risk or maybe it’s no risk at all because of the particular scenario,” Hamrick noted in an interview with HousingWire.

Julia Curran, senior managing director of residential AI products at SitusAMC, said the manufacturer uses AI to re-underwrite closed loans in the secondary market, checking regulatory and underwriting guidelines as well as data accuracy before loans are reviewed for securitization.

In a recent development, according to Curran, SitusAMC builds AI agents around processes established by human subject matter experts and tests their results against loans previously reviewed by people. She noted the company runs repeated tests until the system reaches at least 95% accuracy.

Sources indicate that but the technology still needs the human touch. Curran said the system sends blank or inconsistent fields to human reviewers, and final credit decisions require judgments that cannot be reduced to individual data points.

“A final credit decision shouldn’t be made by the machine because there’s other things to consider besides the specific data points,” Curran noted.

Hamrick added: “Companies that fully rely on AI are potentially going to have misses in some other areas where a human might have been able to make a different decision.”.

Industry observers note that curran also warned about the AI model supplying information not supported or provided by the documents submitted. She described a case in which a model supplied a solar panel number that was not included in a particular loan file. The answer was correct, but the system had apparently drawn on information from other files.

According to recent reports, “Even though it’s right, I don’t want that answer,” Curran said. “I want to stay within the four walls of this file.”.

The executives stated lenders should test AI against established human processes before relying on it for underwriting.

Recent findings suggest that hamrick recommended introducing the technology in one part of the workflow at a time, comparing its results with human reviews before expanding its use. She also said lenders should prepare employees for changes by retraining them for tasks that require more human intervention.

“The best thing that we can do as leaders is look where the technology can ultimately take over, and then take the folks that are doing those roles and train them to be better at the things that require more human intervention,” she stated.

Recent findings suggest that curran remarked quality control requires testing models across different loan types and scenarios. SitusAMC maintains a test bank of hundreds of previously reviewed loans, including purchases, refinances, adjustable-rate mortgages and loans with rate buydowns. When a model changes, the firm runs its prompts against the test bank to check whether results remain consistent.

In a recent development, these tests add costs that lenders may overlook. Curran said companies should ask AI vendors how their systems were developed, whether subject matter experts helped establish the processes and whether ongoing regression testing is in place.

“You want the same answer every time,” Curran stated. “The process of taking a non-deterministic process and making it deterministic takes a lot of time and effort.”.

  • Recent findings suggest that the department’s Arson/Bomb Squad is now using a Spot robot from Boston Dynamics, bought with a Federal Emergency Management Agency grant that the Seattle City Council approved in April after a review of privacy and security risks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 17, 2026 at 11:43 amNovember 17, 2026 at 11:43 am.

According to recent reports, seattle police already have a dog that sniffs out tech. Now they’ve got a piece of tech that looks like a dog.

Recent findings suggest that the department’s Arson/Bomb Squad is now using a Spot robot from Boston Dynamics, bought with a Federal Emergency Management Agency grant that the Seattle City Council approved in April after a review of privacy and security risks. Bomb technicians can steer the robot from nearly a mile away to inspect suspicious devices, open doors and move possible explosives into safe containers, SPD said in a blog post last week.

It’s a big upgrade for the squad, which has handled more than 600 calls so far this year. SPD’s main bomb robot is nearly 20 years old, weighs more than 100 pounds and rolls on tracks, and it can only be hauled around in the squad’s mobile workshop. Spot weighs under 100 pounds, climbs stairs and rides in a pickup truck that bomb techs drive daily.

SPD also spelled out what Spot won’t do.

The robot will only be used for explosive threats in the city and at the port, and it won’t carry a weapon. SPD noted a weapon would go against Boston Dynamics’ rules for its robots. Spot’s 360-degree camera sends an encrypted live feed to the operator but doesn’t record or use facial recognition.

The only thing the robot does on its own is open a door, after an operator lines it up. As one bomb technician put it in SPD’s post, Spot will “be as dumb in 10 years as it is today.”.

It’s not the first time SPD has turned to a four-legged partner for tech-related work.

Nala, an electronic storage detection K9 — profiled by GeekWire in 2024 — is trained to smell a chemical compound used in making electronics. The Labrador retriever helps SPD’s Internet Crimes Against Children task force find hidden phones, hard drives and micro SD cards during warrant searches. Her handler, Det. Daljit Gill, told GeekWire at the time that Nala turns up a device human searchers missed about 30% of the time.

Spot appears decidedly less cuddly.

Industry observers note that boston Dynamics, maker of backflipping Atlas humanoids and other viral-video robots, first unveiled the robodog in 2015. A smaller, all-electric version followed a year later.

The machines have long stirred dystopian unease. A 2017 “Black Mirror” episode featured killer robot dogs inspired by the manufacturer’s designs. Still, Spot has turned up in friendlier settings: then-Amazon CEO Jeff Bezos walked one at the company’s MARS conference in 2018 — a scene described by GeekWire’s Alan Boyle as featuring the “anxiety-inducing” robot.

In a recent development, police departments have embraced the robots, too. More than 60 bomb squads and SWAT teams in the U.S. and Canada use Spot, Bloomberg reported last year, including a regional bomb unit in Portland. New York police returned one in 2021 after public backlash, then brought the robots back two years later.

Recent findings suggest that back in Seattle, SPD’s bomb technicians see more potential uses down the road, according to the department’s post, including communicating and observing from a distance as part of de-escalation. For now, Spot’s job is limited to explosives.

And the robot won’t be getting a new name, SPD said, “because it is not a toy, or a dog, even though it kind of looks like both.”.

The Single Asset Vault amendment on the XRP Ledger is getting closer to activation on the mainnet as validator support builds for the network’s preparation to enable better DeFi functionality.

In a recent development, according to data from XRPScan, the SingleAssetVault amendment, or XLS-65, has received yes votes from 25 of 35 trusted validators, right now standing at 71.43% consensus as of November 18, 2026. It needs more than 80% of 35 votes (29) to start its 14-day countdown to activation. That means it needs four more votes to get there and could reach the magic number before the end of 2026.

Sources indicate that the XRP Ledger’s amendment process requires a proposed amendment to be approved by more than 80% of trusted validators for 14 days before it is implemented. Validator support may shift during this time, and if the required 80% threshold is lost, activation may be delayed.

Recent findings suggest that the Single Asset Vault amendment creates a structure for aggregating assets from multiple depositors and is intended to be used with the on-chain Lending Protocol. The amendment introduces a Vault object that defines the state of a tokenized vault, and the Vault entry is one of the ledger entry types it provides.

The Vault object holds key information such as available assets, shares, total value, and other relevant information. Users can create a Vault object with the VaultCreate transaction; the Vault object is tracked in an Owner Directory owned by the Vault Owner account.

In a recent development, the XRP Ledger lending amendment has gained additional yes votes. According to XRPScan, the LendingProtocolV1_1 amendment, also known as XLS-66, has received 24 yes votes out of 35 trusted validators, meaning it has 68.57% consensus as of November 18, 2026. It needs more than 80% of the 35 votes (29) to trigger a 14-day activation countdown.

This implies that there are five votes left for it to reach this threshold, with the possibility of it securing the required number of votes before the end of 2026 as well.

According to XRP enthusiasts, LendingProtocolV1_1 represents the biggest amendment for unlocking capital and liquidity on the XRP Ledger and is anticipated by institutional and retail users.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 17:22 EST / NOVEMBER 23 2026.

Enterprise data security startup Matters.AI today declared that it has raised $12 million in new funding as it expands its business in North America.

Matters.AI offers a platform called the AI Security Engineer for Data that is designed to protect sensitive data used by employees, artificial intelligence systems and AI agents across the enterprise. Formerly known as OptiQ.AI, the organization has teams in the San Francisco Bay Area and Bengaluru, India.

AI agents, the company argues, now have the same access to enterprise data as the employees who run them. Visibility into who or what is using that data is missing from most data security tools, according to Matters.AI, leaving security teams to connect alerts from separate tools by hand.

Sources indicate that security teams using Matters.AI get one place to see where sensitive data resides, where it has traveled and who or what has accessed it. Data is tracked across cloud environments, on-premises systems, software-as-a-service applications, endpoints and browsers. The company’s AI analyzes the context of that data and the intent behind each use.

It has been revealed that underneath that view, sensitive data across the data estate is discovered and classified, according to the organization. Matters.AI also uses patented fingerprinting, built on large language models, to follow data as it moves between systems.

Recent findings suggest that insider risk and compliance risk are identified by correlating four signals, those being data sensitivity, misconfiguration, access and intent. Within policies set by the security team, the AI Security Engineer for Data is designed to gather the evidence on a flagged risk before remediating it on its own.

The platform is being pitched as a way to bring together work that enterprises typically buy as five separate products: data security posture management, data detection and response, database activity monitoring, data loss prevention and insider risk management.

Industry observers note that coming into its new funding round, Matters.AI has been deployed at more than 50 organizations. Customers include major financial institutions, brokerage and asset management firms, large retailers and digital media and entertainment platforms, the tech giant claims.

“Enterprises want to move fast with AI, but no one can trust an agent with data they cannot follow,” Harsh Sahu, co-founder and chief technology officer of Matters.AI, stated in the manufacturer’s announcement. According to Sahu, the platform works across petabytes of data and billions of access events a day.

Co-founder and Chief Executive Keshava Murthy argued that security teams do not need “another tool telling them something might be wrong,” adding that they instead need a system that can investigate a problem and take action.

Tanglin Venture Partners Pte. Ltd. led the pre-Series A round, with IIFL Fintech Fund, Piper Serica’s Bharat Tech Fund, Foster Ventures and Tetration Ventures also participating. Existing investors Kalaari Capital and Endiya Partners also invested in the round. The pair co-led a $4.75 million seed round confirmed in October 2025, when Matters.AI also disclosed an earlier $1.5 million pre-seed round led by Better Capital and Carya Venture Partners.

Sankalp Gupta, managing partner at Tanglin Venture Partners, said that rather than “adding another layer of alerts, the team is rethinking how enterprise data security operates.”.

In a recent development, research and development in data lineage, autonomous investigation, endpoint and browser intelligence and the prevention of sensitive data misuse by AI agents will be the focus of the money raised. Including the new funding, Matters.AI has raised $18.25 million to date.

  • In a recent development, employees with strong strategic clarity know that AI is a priority, understand the strategy and their role in it, and have clear guidance on what to do with the time AI saves.
  • These are among the findings of For Asia-Pacific, Strategic Clarity Is the Key to Value, BCG's second annual APAC AI at Work report, based on a survey of 6,349 employees in Australia, China, India, Indonesia, Japan, Malaysia, Singapore, South Korea, and Thailand.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, SINGAPORE, Nov. 23, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Only 20% of employees in Asia Pacific have strong strategic clarity about AI, according to a newly introduced report from Boston Consulting Group (BCG). Among regular AI users in APAC, strong strategic clarity lifts the number of employees reporting measurable business impact by 22 percentage points, versus 4 percentage points for access to AI tools.

In a recent development, employees with strong strategic clarity know that AI is a priority, understand the strategy and their role in it, and have clear guidance on what to do with the time AI saves. Communication also shapes trust. Where employees say leadership communicates very clearly about AI, 61% fully trust leadership, compared with 3% where communication is not clear.

These are among the findings of For Asia-Pacific, Strategic Clarity Is the Key to Value, BCG's second annual APAC AI at Work report, based on a survey of 6,349 employees in Australia, China, India, Indonesia, Japan, Malaysia, Singapore, South Korea, and Thailand. Respondents in Australia, India, and Japan were surveyed for the global AI at Work 2026 study of 11,749 employees, published in June, and the rest in September and October.

Sources indicate that AI use is now near-universal across Asia Pacific. Eighty-five percent of employees use it regularly, up from 78% in 2025 and in line with 84% globally. Japan saw the sharpest increase over the past year, from 51% to 79%, while India leads the region at 96%.

Far fewer employees use AI deeply. Only 26% use it regularly and for at least half of their daily tasks. Those employees save an average of 14.3 hours a week, compared with 6.2 hours for people who use AI less than a few times a week.

Many companies are going beyond deploying AI tools. Sixty-nine percent of APAC employees say their organization uses AI to reshape end-to-end work, compared with 57% globally, while 45% say it is used to invent newly introduced business models. At companies that reshape or invent with AI, 60% of employees report measurable business impact, compared with 43% at companies that only deploy AI tools.

In a recent development, "Getting AI into employees' hands was the easy part, and Asia Pacific has largely done it," remarked Jeff Walters, managing director and senior partner at BCG and a coauthor of the report. "The measurable impact comes from what happens next, when companies rebuild how work gets done around AI.".

Industry observers note that the report also finds a "joy paradox," with work becoming both more demanding and more enjoyable. Among employees with strong strategic clarity, 76% enjoy their work more and 47% report a higher cognitive load, versus 30% and 21% with no clarity. Only 7% of them are anxious about AI, against 19% without clarity.

"Each market in Asia Pacific needs its own playbook, but three priorities hold everywhere," mentioned Romain de Laubier, Asia-Pacific regional chair at BCG X and a coauthor of the report. "Make strategic clarity the number one priority, measure the value AI creates rather than how much it is used, and put the guardrails in place to use it responsibly.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 11:57 amNovember 17, 2026 at 12:33 pm.

Microsoft is a partner and investor in both OpenAI and Anthropic, and it sells their AI models to its own customers. But another role was on full display during the organization’s Ignite keynote Tuesday: competitor.

“Simply stated, anything you can do in Claude or ChatGPT, you can do better with Copilot and for less,” remarked Judson Althoff, CEO of Microsoft’s commercial business, during the opening keynote at the manufacturer’s annual conference for IT professionals and business customers in San Francisco.

Jacob Andreou, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, went further. “We’ve all seen Anthropic and OpenAI embrace documents, slides, and spreadsheets, but their simplified viewers and editors force compromise on power and collaboration,” he stated.

Industry observers note that the full versions of Word, Excel and PowerPoint inside Copilot are included in the subscription. “That means that Copilot is the only way to draft a PowerPoint presentation without spinning a meter,” Andreou mentioned.

Microsoft’s cost comparison: Andreou backed up the pitch with a chart of estimated monthly costs per business user, including subscription and usage fees. It put Copilot at $30 for an “everyday” AI user, compared with $81 for ChatGPT and $205 for Claude.

For “advanced” owners of each manufacturer’s agent tools, it highlighted $96 for Copilot, $149 for ChatGPT and $299 for Claude. Most of the Claude figure is estimated usage charges on top of Anthropic’s $20 enterprise seat.

Recent findings suggest that the numbers come from research Microsoft commissioned and paid for from GigaOm, based on testing Microsoft ran in October on modeled workloads. They reflect enterprise pricing, which adds usage charges to a per-seat fee, not the flat monthly subscriptions that individuals pay for ChatGPT and Claude.

According to recent reports, partners and rivals: The pitch comes as Anthropic expands into Microsoft’s core business. Last week it introduced newly introduced Claude-based tools for spreadsheets and whiteboards that compete more directly with Office. The company is expected to make its IPO this week, putting new scrutiny on its financials and long-term growth prospects.

Recent findings suggest that the companies’ products are also intertwined. Anthropic’s Claude for Microsoft 365, for example, lets people use Claude inside Office apps for tasks such as sorting email and creating slide decks.

It has been revealed that the product has less than a tenth as many weekly consumers as the paid version of Copilot in Office, The Information reported Monday, citing internal Microsoft data. Andreou is one of the executives who see that as a sign Microsoft can keep customers from switching, the report said.

Sources indicate that upcoming MAI models: Microsoft AI also released a new batch of its own MAI models, built to compete with OpenAI and Anthropic for a fraction of the price. It’s a notable stance, given that Microsoft still sells their models, too. On the same stage, CEO Satya Nadella announced that OpenAI’s GPT-6.2, released Tuesday morning, is now available in Microsoft Foundry.

It has been revealed that the lineup includes MAI Code 2, available in GitHub Copilot starting Tuesday. Microsoft claims it delivers 96% of the coding performance of Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5 at 5% of the price, on benchmarks Microsoft chose.

Microsoft also introduced MAI Cyber 2 Flash, a security model it notes matches OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra on one benchmark at less than 2% of the cost per task. Other fresh models cover image editing, live speech and transcription.

The other newly introduced business: MAI Licensed Weights. Companies can take a Microsoft AI model, customize it with their own data and run it in their own Azure environment, with help from Microsoft’s Frontier Company consulting arm. AT&T used an earlier version of the program, Custom Models, to build a MAI model for 5G network analytics.

It’s the latest step in Microsoft’s push for what Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman has called “long term self-sufficiency,” which started with seven homegrown models at Build in June.

Sources indicate that keeping costs in check: The cost theme ran through the keynote. In a demo, Althoff highlighted Copilot building a keynote outline, a slide deck and a customer tracker for a retail conference, plus an agent he named Amelia to keep the work going.

The cost of his two-hour Sunday session: about 10,000 credits, or roughly $100. Althoff presented that as a bargain compared with the staff time it would have taken: “my team hits the ground running for NRF without me bothering them,” he mentioned.

Industry observers note that microsoft is also selling tools to keep that bill in check. A new Agent 365 Business Analytics feature demonstrates business leaders what’s driving their AI spending and what they’re getting for it, and a companion Cost Management tool lets IT set spending policies and get alerts. Microsoft cited a McKinsey survey in which 93% of respondents reported exceeding their AI budgets.

According to recent reports, in another notable announcement, Microsoft and Salesforce unveiled “Copilotforce,” bringing Salesforce customer data and actions into Copilot, Teams and Fabric. The Copilot plugin is available in preview.

Earlier, Nadella opened the keynote by addressing last week’s global Outlook outage.

#99551. Mortgage headlines aren’t as big a concern as your cost per closing

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (967 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Housingwire ↗ Open Full Page

Mortgage headlines aren’t as big a concern as your cost per closing

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (967 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you run a real estate team, several weeks ago you probably saw and heard the chatter about potential rate hikes as high as 9% in 2027.
  • Freddie Mac had the 30-year fixed at 7.28% on Oct.
  • Sources indicate that the Real Estate Agent Facebook groups were bubbling about this in the comments.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you run a real estate team, several weeks ago you probably saw and heard the chatter about potential rate hikes as high as 9% in 2027.

I understand why it spread. Freddie Mac had the 30-year fixed at 7.28% on Oct. 1, up from 6.01% in February and the Fed raised rates in September for the first time since 2023. If everything moves the wrong way at once, 9% could sound possible.

Sources indicate that the Real Estate Agent Facebook groups were bubbling about this in the comments. It is likely causing some anxiety for many agents.

It helps to look at what it would actually take. Cotality’s chief economist, Selma Hepp, raised 9% on CNBC as a worst case, not a forecast. HousingWire’s Logan Mohtashami laid out the math: the 10-year would have to push past 6%, and mortgage spreads would have to widen well beyond the roughly 2% they sit at today. That requires a hot economy, oil prices that stay high and a Fed that keeps hiking past what markets expect, all lasting well into next year. September’s jobs report indicated 29,000 latest jobs, which already works against the hot-economy part.

Sources indicate that so I wouldn’t proposal around 9%. I also wouldn’t plan around rates falling back to 6% anytime soon. The Fed’s own projections show no cuts in 2027, and the Mortgage Bankers Association expects rates to stay close to where they are.

It has been revealed that A crash needs forced sellers, and we don’t have many. Homeowners with a mortgage carry an average loan-to-value of about 44%, and only around 2% are underwater, according to Cotality. That isn’t 2008.

Industry observers note that what we do have is fewer deals. In early October, pending sales were about 10% less than the year before, and purchase applications were down 14%. Those applications turn into closings 30 to 90 days later, so a lot of teams have been looking at a softer first quarter. At today’s rate, the payment that covered a $400,000 loan in February covers about $357,000 now. Same buyer, same budget, about 11% less loan.

It has been revealed that prices mostly hold, and the deal count shrinks. I think of 2027 as a consolidation year rather than a crash year.

In August, I wrote here that cost-per-lead is the wrong number to run a team on, and that cost-per-closed deal is the one that tells you the truth. A slow year is when that stops being a philosophy and turns into a real potential problem.

Recent findings suggest that most of what a team spends to generate business is fixed. The ad campaign, vendor contracts, the ISA hours and the coaching all get billed whether deals close or not. When conversion falls, none of those invoices get smaller.

Say a team spends $6,000 a month on lead generation and closes 12 deals a quarter from it. That’s $1,500 per closing. Then buyer conversion slips, and the same spend produces nine closings. Now each closing costs $2,000. Nothing on the invoice changed, and every deal got a third more expensive.

That’s the exposure I’d worry about: a cost structure built for a 6.5% market, running in a 7.5% one.

The gap between a team that knows its number and one that doesn’t gets much wider when volume drops.

You can’t control the 10-year Treasury. These are the things you can control though:.

It has been revealed that find your cost per closing by source. Add up everything you spend on each lead source, including ad spend, platform and referral fees, ISA time and software, and divide it by the closed transactions that source produced over the last 12 months. Use closings, not appointments or signed agreements. Most team leads I talk to have never broken this out by source, and the answer usually surprises them.

Stress-test it at a lower deal count. Run the same numbers assuming 20% fewer closings. Any source that ends up costing more per closing than your net is one to fix or cut now, while you still have room to choose.

Shift your mix toward sellers and your sphere. Buyers are the first to stall when rates jump. Sellers still have to move for new jobs, divorces, estates, and growing families, whatever the rate happens to be, and your past clients are sitting on real equity. If most of your pipeline is buyer leads, 2027 will hurt more than it should.

In a recent development, lengthen your nurture instead of cutting it. The buyer who is priced out at 7.5% may be ready at 6.75%. If your follow-up ends at 90 days, someone else gets that deal if rates turn, and you end up paying for the same lead twice.

Give your agents training so they can handle these clients. Don’t promise rates will fall. Understand the concern first, then help the buyer evaluate actual numbers without treating a forecast as a fact.

2023 had the fewest existing-home sales since 1995. The teams I watched hold up through it weren’t the ones that guessed right about rates. They were the ones that knew what each closing cost them and kept moving money toward what was working.

There will be another very scary hot topic after this one, and another after that. The best hedge against all of them is the same: know your cost per closing, and build a pipeline that doesn’t depend on buyers feeling good about rates.

Robyn Thompson DeSantos is the founder and CEO of Ascension Group, a business solutions and management tech giant for real estate team leaders and brokers.
